pronunciation.note: Ọbalúayé is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute accents on ú and é are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acutes preserving high tones, while grave accents would mark low tones. The dot below ọ distinguishes open [ɔ] from close [o].

domains.title: Father of the World
domains.subtitle: Disease, Healing, and the Earth
domains.lead: Ọbalúayé is the orixá who both strikes and heals. He governs infectious disease — above all smallpox — and the earth that receives the body after death. The hand that sends sickness can also lift it, and those who survive what he sends become his healers. In the diaspora he walks as an old man on crutches, wrapped in burlap, with two dogs at his side.

cards.name: Disease and Pestilence
cards.desc: Smallpox, leprosy, and epidemic illness walk in his shadow — he is the scourge no wall keeps out.

cards.name: Healing
cards.desc: The same hand that sends illness can remove it; his priests are herbalists, and his broom sweeps sickness from the house.

cards.name: Earth and the Grave
cards.desc: He rules the soil that receives the dead and the smallest beings that break the body down.

cards.name: Survival
cards.desc: Those who survive his illness often become his children for life — survival itself is the initiation.

symbols.name: Crutches
symbols.meaning: His diaspora attribute, marking lameness and the limit of the human body.

symbols.name: Burlap or sackcloth
symbols.meaning: Poverty, humility, and the rough texture of illness and recovery.

symbols.name: Two dogs
symbols.meaning: His messengers and guardians at the boundary of sickness and health.

symbols.name: Earth-coloured beads
symbols.meaning: Brown, black, and purple beads that link him to soil and burial.

symbols.name: The ritual broom
symbols.meaning: The broom that sweeps a house clean of sickness — his oldest instrument of healing.

mythology.lead: Ọbalúayé's mythology is not a heroic cycle but an oral canon — Yoruba praise poetry carried across the Atlantic and kept in patakís, the teaching stories of Santería and Candomblé. The versions disagree in detail and agree in meaning: affliction is real, the earth sends it, and survival rightly borne becomes holiness.

myths.title: The King Cast Down
myths.text: In the most widely told patakís of the Cuban canon, Babalú-Ayé was not always a beggar. He was a king — some say the proudest of the orixás — who grew contemptuous of the sick, or hoarded the secrets of healing, until Olodumare's judgment fell on him: sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, and exile from every door. Only the dogs stayed, licking his wounds, and in their rough tenderness lay the first medicine. Cast out, he walked the earth as the poorest of the poor, and the humiliation remade him: the god who had despised affliction became its master and its cure. His modern collectors — Mason in Four New World Yoruba Rituals, Murphy in Santería: African Spirits in America — record versions that differ in detail; all agree on the moral: the healer must know the body from inside affliction, and pride is the first disease he treats.

myths.title: The Dogs and the Hidden Path
myths.text: Dogs belong to Ọbalúayé on both continents because they live at the boundary he owns — between the village and the bush, the healthy and the sick, the living and the earth that takes them. In Yoruba teaching the dog runs ahead on paths men cannot see; in diaspora patakís it is the dog who leads the sufferer to the stream where the healing leaves grow, or who carries the message between the sick person's door and the orixá's. His devotees keep the image literally: two dogs stand beside the old man on crutches in every altar figure, and dog imagery runs through his beadwork and his cloth. The myth encodes the practical work of healing in an epidemic age — one must follow signs that do not speak in human language, keep low to the ground, and trust the guide that never strays far from the earth that sends both the sickness and the herb.

myths.title: At the Crossroads of Saint Lazarus
myths.text: In Cuban Santería, Babalú Ayé appears as an old beggar at the crossroads, leaning on crutches, accompanied by dogs — and the image is liturgical as much as narrative. His feast falls on 17 December, the Catholic day of Saint Lazarus, and on that night tens of thousands of Cubans make the pilgrimage to the shrine of San Lázaro at El Rincón, many crawling the last distance on their knees, leaving offerings of roasted corn, dry wine, and herbs: the largest religious procession in the country. The beggar's shape is theology: illness can reduce anyone — king or scholar — to dependence, and dependence rightly borne is a form of holiness. The crossroads is his because sickness is a crossroads, the body at the point where the road forks toward death or back toward life, and his dogs are posted there to guide the choosing.

myths.title: Sọpọnná and the Name Not Spoken
myths.text: In Yorubaland the smallpox deity was spoken of with greater care than any other orisha. The safe title was Ọbalúayé — 'master of the world' — while the name Sọpọnná, attested in the Ifá corpus and early ethnography, was dangerous to say aloud during an epidemic, since naming the disease might summon it (Idowu, Olódùmarè; Bascom, Ifá Divination). When mission churches and colonial medical authorities attacked 'smallpox worship' in the early twentieth century, the cult went underground and re-emerged across the ocean, re-dressed as Babalú-Ayé beneath the cloak of Saint Lazarus. The concealment is itself the theology: the god of invisible killers keeps his name hidden, and survives by being renamed — a deity whose power is secrecy learned, under persecution, to live by it across an ocean.

lore.syncretism: In Brazil he became Obaluaiê or Omolu, syncretised with São Lázaro and São Roque — the Catholic saints of sores and plague, whose images (Lazarus covered in ulcers at the rich man's gate, Roch displaying the sore on his thigh) mapped almost perfectly onto the orixá. In Cuba he is Babalú Ayé under the cloak of San Lázaro, and across the wider diaspora he keeps the same two saintly disguises. The mapping was not camouflage alone: it was translation. Catholic hagiography already told his essential story — the despised sick man at the gate who is closer to God than the healthy — and the African canon simply read the saints as another telling of the king cast down. His modern afterlife is global: his earth-colored beads appear wherever the Yoruba diaspora sings, and each December his pilgrim crowds at El Rincón outdraw nearly every other feast in the Americas.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ọbalúayé's legacy is the theology of illness. In Yoruba and Afro-Atlantic thought, sickness is not mere biological accident; it is a message, a punishment, or a calling, and those who survive smallpox — or the modern afflictions that have inherited his domain — often dedicate their survival to him. The old man's image governed the public meaning of disease in the Americas for centuries: the sick were not hidden but displayed, at the crossroads, on crutches, wrapped in sackcloth, with dogs. In the age of global pandemics his mythology has gained uncomfortable new resonance: the earth still sends plagues, the boundary between health and sickness is still thinner than medicine admits, and the crowds at El Rincón each December are, among other things, the largest annual public acknowledgment anywhere that we are all, sooner or later, his.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọbalúayé is the god nobody wants until they need him. He is smallpox scars, crutches, the cough that will not stop, the fever that empties the world. And yet he is also the one who knows the herb, the cool stream, the moment when the crisis turns.

To approach him is to accept the fragility of the body. He does not promise that illness is meaningful, only that it is real and that survival is possible. In a culture that often hides disability and death, Ọbalúayé stands at the crossroads in sackcloth, leaning on crutches, accompanied by dogs. He makes poverty and sickness visible — and in making them visible, he begins to heal them.

lore.archaeology: Ọbalúayé left no inscriptions and no ancient monuments — his material culture is the living altar. In Cuba, the casa-templo and the home altar keep his figure: the old man in burlap on crutches, flanked by dogs, ringed with gourds of grain and bundles of his herbs; the great pilgrimage church of San Lázaro at El Rincón, Santiago de las Vegas, receives his votive offerings by the thousand each December. In Bahia, Candomblé ilé shrines preserve the cowrie strings, earth-colored beads, and consecrated brooms of Obaluaiê, documented by ethnographers since the nineteenth century and by Verger's surveys. Behind the diaspora altar stands the West African substrate: the shrines and guarded groves of the smallpox deity described by Idowu and Bascom, suppressed under colonial medicine, surviving in the secrecy his theology always claimed as its own. His oldest 'excavation site' is the epidemic graveyard itself.
